aligned_items: Both the blind-first driver and the official Rust implementations keep the cpufreq driver name as `cpufreq-dt` and preserve the generic callbacks `init`, `target_index`, `get`, `suspend`, `verify`, and `register_em`.
Both designs keep long-lived OPP/freq-table/clock resources in per-policy state rather than in long-lived probe-global storage.
Both designs preserve the `cpu0` then `cpu` regulator-name fallback semantics from the C driver.
Both designs keep `online` and `offline` as lightweight paths and rely on `target_index` plus OPP `set_rate` for frequency changes.
unaligned_items: The official initial and mature Rust files model `cpufreq-dt` as an OF-matched platform driver with no driver-wide shared config, while the blind-first rerun models probe-time shared state explicitly and registers the cpufreq core through `RegistrationConfig` plus `driver_data`.

The official initial and mature Rust files do not model `cpufreq_dt_platform_data` callback plumbing or the `cpufreq_dt_pdev_register` seam inside the driver file, while the blind-first rerun adds a thin public seam in `rust/kernel/cpufreq_dt.rs` and keeps callback-aware shared config.

The official initial and mature Rust files rely on driver-file `unsafe` for CPU-device access and policy resource publication, while the blind-first rerun moves those operations behind safe abstractions and keeps the driver layer at zero `unsafe` and zero direct bindings use.
The official initial and mature Rust files keep `BOOST_ENABLED=true` with a no-op `set_boost`, while the blind-first rerun currently leaves boost handling unimplemented in the driver trait surface.

functional_differences.detail: The blind-first rerun intentionally covers more of the C gold standard than the official initial Rust file by carrying the shared C seam, runtime registration flags, and optional platform-data callback plumbing.
The C gold driver sets `.set_boost = cpufreq_boost_set_sw`, and the official Rust file exposes boost-related trait surface, while the blind-first rerun currently does not implement a boost path.

In mcimx7d-sabre runtime, the C baseline emits `platform cpufreq-dt: deferred probe pending`, while the Rust candidate reaches the same unbound platform-device state without the same dmesg line. Because neither run reaches policy sysfs, this remains an unvalidated runtime difference candidate.

engineering_differences: The blind-first rerun adds `present_cpus()` / `for_each_present()` / callback-scoped CPU device access in `rust/kernel/cpu.rs`.
The blind-first rerun adds immutable typed platform data reads in `rust/kernel/platform.rs`.
The blind-first rerun adds regulator RAII and CPU-device OPP table helpers in `rust/kernel/opp.rs`.
The blind-first rerun adds safe policy resource publication and runtime-configurable cpufreq registration in `rust/kernel/cpufreq.rs`.
The blind-first rerun keeps driver-layer `unsafe` at zero, which is stricter than both the official initial and mature Rust files.
old_tree_constraints: The local `ARM_IMX_CPUFREQ_DT depends on CPUFREQ_DT || CPUFREQ_DT_RUST` patch is benchmark harness switching integration only.
The benchmark configs disable `CONFIG_MODVERSIONS` so Rust remains selectable on this tree.
The sabrelite runtime had to move to a `multi_v7_defconfig`-derived ARMv7 baseline to avoid old-tree ARM/Rust helper link failures.
A host-side LLVM compatibility layer was required to satisfy the tree's clang requirement without altering system libraries.
workflow_defects: The first runtime harness revision staged a host-architecture busybox into the ARM guest initramfs and therefore failed before any cpufreq observation.
The first runtime launcher revision did not normalize CR in the serial verdict marker and could hang after guest halt without explicit QEMU stop logic.
An intermediate build command used an overlong dtb target path, which was a local execution mistake rather than a code or tree constraint.
official_evolution: From `06149d8...` to current-tree mature, the official Rust file mostly changed API spelling and tree integration details, such as `c_str!` to `c"..."`, `property_present()` through `fwnode()`, `DEFAULT_TRANSITION_LATENCY_NS`, and `PinInit`-style probe return shape.
No major structural evolution was observed between the official initial and mature files with respect to shared config, platdata callback plumbing, or driver-layer unsafe concentration.

assessment.scope_vs_c_gold: The blind-first rerun expands beyond the official initial Rust scope toward the C gold standard by carrying the shared C seam and callback-aware registration, but still has an open boost-path gap and no runtime policy-level validation.
assessment.remaining_gap_to_official_mature: The blind-first rerun is more ambitious on engineering safety and C-scope coverage, but it diverges structurally from the mature official file and still lacks runtime proof for the deeper paths it targets.
assessment.tool_failure_judgment: Partial. The workflow successfully produced a zero-unsafe blind-first driver plus supporting abstractions, but runtime evidence remained capped by baseline observability gaps and one open runtime difference candidate.
